clue.text: Small fruit — but these could kill you!

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
pears are a fruit, in the plural

explanation.surface: A warning that some innocent-looking little fruit is deadly poisonous.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark and 'these' make the second half sound like a comment on the fruit; it is a separate definition of SPEARS, weapons that really could kill you.
explanation.definitionFit: Spears are thrusting or thrown weapons, so a loose descriptive phrase about lethal objects fits them.

clue.text: Mountain climbing: something that enlivens a sort of relationship

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective that names this sort of relationship

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means reading upwards, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: an alp is a high mountain, as in the Alps
a tonic is anything that invigorates or bucks you up

explanation.surface: A mountaineering trip recommended as the thing to put the spark back into a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon suggests the mountain climbing is itself the enlivening thing; really the mountain goes upwards to give PLA, followed by TONIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A platonic relationship is an affectionate friendship without romance or sex, so the word names one kind of relationship.

clue.text: Kind of parliamentary sitting, entirely disorganised thing

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective describing this kind of sitting

parts.note: all = entirely, as in 'all alone'

indicators.note: something disorganised has lost its proper order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: A jibe that a certain kind of parliamentary session is a thoroughly chaotic affair.
explanation.walkthrough: An all-night sitting is when the House of Commons debates through the night to push business through.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliamentary sessions that continue through until morning are described as all-night sittings in British political reporting.

clue.text: A pun with grass? Ridiculous — it's a sort of pea!

indicators.note: a ridiculous arrangement is an absurd one, so the letters are put into a silly new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters; 'with' just joins the two parts

explanation.surface: Someone groaning at a feeble joke about grass, then pointing out it is really about a pea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pun' pulls attention toward wordplay on the surface, yet 'A pun with grass' is simply nine letters waiting to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The sugar snap is a variety of garden pea with a sweet, edible pod eaten whole.

clue.text: In favour of pipes and other manufactured items

parts.note: pro = for, in favour of, as in pros and cons
ducts are pipes or channels carrying air or fluid

explanation.surface: Someone declaring support for pipes and every other manufactured article.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads pipes as one of the manufactured items; 'and other' in fact joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Products are goods made in a factory or workshop, the ordinary synonym for things manufactured for sale.

clue.text: This could provide power in the future, corruptly, or get penalty in holding first of elections

definitions.text: This could provide power in the future

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece sits within the other
done corruptly means twisted from its proper form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter only

parts.note: the opening letter of Elections

explanation.surface: A warning about corrupt power: rig the elections now or face a penalty later.
explanation.walkthrough: The election story hides a physics term; the E goes inside the fourteen fodder letters and the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Potential energy is stored energy, held by position or state, that can be released later as work.

clue.text: Excursion requiring ID to be organised with party

indicators.note: organising means putting things into a new arrangement, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: used literally
anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: An outing where identification must be sorted out along with the group going.
explanation.walkthrough: ID looks like paperwork for the trip, but its two letters join PARTY as material for the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A day trip is a short outing there and back within a single day, an everyday kind of excursion.

clue.text: Moon ring is also finally hidden

indicators.note: when the final letter is concealed from view, the word loses its ending

parts.note: to ring someone is to call them
used literally
too = also
TOO with its last letter out of sight

explanation.surface: A lunar ring that turns out also to be out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moon ring' reads as a halo round the moon, but the definition stops at 'Moon'; ring is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Callisto is one of the four large satellites of Jupiter discovered by Galileo.

clue.text: Steed lay, after exercising gently

indicators.note: exercising works things over and puts them through their paces, so the letters get moved about

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A horse lying down quietly after a workout.
explanation.walkthrough: The horse and its exercise make a complete little scene, so the definition hides at the far end as a single adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: To move sedately is to go in a calm, unhurried, dignified way, close in sense to softly.

clue.text: Supporter with only a little alcohol or sugar in window

parts.note: a fan is a supporter of a team or star

parts.words: with only a little alcohol or sugar
parts.note: light beer or light yoghurt has reduced alcohol or sugar

explanation.surface: A fan drinking low-alcohol or low-sugar drinks in a window seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' sounds like part of the scene but merely links the wordplay to the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanlight is the small, often semicircular pane set above a door, a particular kind of glazed opening.

clue.text: This could be blinking English idly muddled about Spain

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other
muddled things are jumbled up, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
anagram fodder, four letters
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: Grumbling about a blinking Englishman lazing around in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blinking' looks like the mild British swearword qualifying the English; it is literal, since an eyelid is what blinks.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyelid is the fold of skin that closes over the eye each time a person blinks, so it performs that action.

clue.text: Iron pot's cooking something very small indeed

indicators.note: cooking transforms its ingredients, and cooking the books means falsifying them, so the letters change order

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters; the apostrophe S counts

explanation.surface: An iron cooking pot turning out a minuscule portion.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'pot's' reads as 'is', but here it supplies an S to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A positron is the antimatter partner of the electron, a subatomic particle and so tiny beyond ordinary measure.

clue.text: Creative type: inside, heart is troubled

indicators.note: inside tells us the letters are found within the run of words that follows

parts.note: the run starts after the first two letters of 'heart' and ends on the first letter of 'troubled'

explanation.surface: The stereotype of the tormented creative, anguished at heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Troubled' looks like an instruction to rearrange 'heart', but ARTIST sits in order across he-ARTIS-T-roubled.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist is a painter, writer or musician, the archetypal person who makes things imaginatively.

clue.text: Give one international player extra golf strokes

definitions.note: the answer is the singular noun for this allowance of strokes

parts.note: to hand something over is to give it
I is the Roman numeral one
a cap is a player picked for a national side, who is awarded a cap

explanation.surface: A request to grant an overseas star some additional shots on the golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give' looks like part of the golf instruction but is the first piece; in Britain an international player is said to win a cap.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer's handicap is the allowance of strokes deducted to level play with stronger opponents.

clue.text: Indicate in advance a stupid American standard

parts.note: used literally
dumb meaning stupid is originally American usage
a rate is a standard or level, as in first-rate

explanation.surface: Someone forecasting that a foolish American benchmark is coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American' qualifies the word for stupid rather than describing a person: dumb as a synonym for stupid is an Americanism.
explanation.definitionFit: To adumbrate is to foreshadow or give a faint outline of something before it happens.

clue.text: Drunkard catches cold, a Glaswegian, maybe

indicators.note: whatever catches something holds it, so one piece ends up inside the other

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunk
C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker in Glasgow coming down with a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catches cold' reads as falling ill; it splits into the container instruction and the letter C. A Glaswegian is a native of Glasgow.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone from Glasgow is an example of a person from Scotland, hence the 'maybe'.

clue.text: One who seeks bowman from the home counties?

parts.note: the Home Counties surround London, in the south-east of England
a bowman shoots with a bow

explanation.surface: Someone looking for an archer who lives in the counties around London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties bordering London; they lie in the south-east, so they supply SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A searcher is a person hunting for something, the agent noun formed from the verb search.

clue.text: Gift made from iron: item worn on the finger

parts.note: of = made from, as in 'a ring of gold'
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
a ring is worn on a finger

explanation.surface: A present of an iron ring for someone's finger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made from iron' looks like a description of the ring; in fact 'made from' is OF and iron is FE.
explanation.definitionFit: An offering is something presented as a present or contribution, especially to a deity or church.

clue.text: Stupid work in airless dairy

indicators.note: something airless has had its air taken out, so those three letters go
in places one piece within another

parts.note: DAIRY minus the letters A, I, R
an op, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: A dull job in a stuffy dairy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Airless' reads as stuffy, but it literally removes the letters of AIR from dairy.
explanation.definitionFit: Dopy is informal for slow-witted or dozy, a close synonym of daft.

clue.text: Maybe removes barriers as means of protection

definitions.note: a verb reading of the answer, DE-FENCES, is invented for the clue
definitions.meaning: read as DE- plus fences, a made-up verb for taking fences down
the ordinary sense: things that guard against attack

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical coinage: to 'de-fence' would be to take the fences down, and 'Maybe' flags that the word is made up.
explanation.definitionFit: Defences are the walls, weapons or measures that guard something against attack.

clue.text: Northern university absorbed in exercise isn't able to provide source of protein

indicators.note: something absorbed in another is taken inside it

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercise
can't = is not able, without its apostrophe
N is the abbreviation for northern
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A northern student too tired from a workout to produce the protein they need.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'isn't able' is dropped, as punctuation always is in crosswords, and the university sits inside that word rather than inside the exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts from the pecan tree supply protein, so each one is a plant-based source of it.

clue.text: Great praise of fruit found all over Australia

indicators.note: something all over another covers it on every side, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: an apple is a fruit
AUS is the abbreviation for Australia

explanation.surface: High acclaim for a fruit grown everywhere in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All over Australia' suggests growing everywhere across the country; here the fruit is placed around the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Applause is clapping or public approval, the acclaim an audience gives a performer.

clue.text: Warned Ed later gets upset

indicators.note: to upset something is to knock it over, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Someone called Ed was cautioned and afterwards became distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Warned' a verb about Ed; it is the definition, and Ed is two letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To alert someone is to make them aware of danger, so a person put on guard has been cautioned.

clue.text: Spliff in jacket

definitions.meaning: a thick double-breasted coat first worn by sailors

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a joint tucked in a pocket; 'in' only links the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Reefer is slang for a cannabis cigarette, and also a thick double-breasted coat worn by sailors.

clue.text: Knight getting drunk: blame on lord?

parts.note: N is the knight in chess notation

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers all over the place, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A knight gets drunk and asks whether the fault lies with his lord.
explanation.walkthrough: N for knight comes from chess notation, where K is already taken by the king.
explanation.definitionFit: A lord is a titled aristocrat, a member of the peerage, which is what a nobleman is.

clue.text: Crimes admitted by atheist society

indicators.note: what is admitted by something is let inside it, so the letters sit within the next words

parts.note: the run starts after 'at' and takes the first letter of 'society'

explanation.surface: A club of non-believers confessing to their offences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admitted' sounds like confessing, which suits crimes; it really means letting the answer inside the words: at-HEIST-S-ociety.
explanation.definitionFit: Heists are robberies, especially daring thefts, and so are particular kinds of criminal offence.

clue.text: Dancers prepared to consume ecstasy to make it to the top once more?

definitions.text: make it to the top once more

indicators.note: consuming something takes it inside, so one piece goes within the other
prepared means worked into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Clubbers ready to take drugs so they can get high again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The top' here is a summit, not a drug high: the definition is climbing again.
explanation.definitionFit: To reascend is to climb up again, so reaching the summit a second time fits it.

clue.text: Stiffness? I had it, visiting doctor with back in agony

parts.note: to doctor is to falsify, to rig
I had = I'd, followed by IT

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of agonY

explanation.surface: A patient with a stiff, painful back going to see the doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is a verb, meaning to tamper with, not a physician; 'visiting' just sets I'D IT beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigidity is the quality of being unbending or inflexible, the abstract noun for being stiff.

clue.text: Punters at zoo maintaining, "It's not the real thing"

definitions.note: a phrase describing the answer, which is chiefly an adjective

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold, so the letters are held within the words before

parts.note: the run takes the last three letters of 'Punters', all of 'at' and the first letter of 'zoo'

explanation.surface: Zoo visitors insisting the animal they are looking at is a fake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maintaining' reads as claiming, introducing the quotation; it is the instruction to hold letters, as in punt-ERS AT Z-oo.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz means substitute or imitation, an inferior stand-in for something genuine.
